title: AI, messy jobs, and the future of schooling
author: Michael J. Petrilli
summary: Michael Petrilli reviews the book Messy Jobs: The Work That AI Cannot Reach by economists Luis Garicano, Jin Li and Yanhui Wu and asks what it means for schools. He says the near-term AI questions in education are about harm, such as cheating and student chats with bots, but the most important ones concern the future of work. The authors argue that jobs made of a single routine task will be automated, whereas knowledge jobs that are tight bundles of complex, conflict-laden tasks will resist automation. Citing David Deming, he stresses that the labor market rewards people who combine analytical thinking with social skill, and that effective AI use requires deep domain expertise. He flags the early-career pipeline as a real problem, since AI can do junior tasks that funded apprenticeship, and ends with the hopeful point that teaching is a caring profession likely to survive and attract stronger candidates.
points: The authors say messiness, meaning bundles of hard-to-specify, interdependent tasks involving people, is what protects knowledge jobs from automation.
Labor-market data show growing demand for workers who combine cognitive and social skills, so schools should not pursue durable skills at the expense of academic expertise.
Spotting AI errors requires deep domain knowledge, which means schools must keep developing students' cognitive capacities and making them experts in something.
If AI absorbs junior-level tasks, firms lose the revenue that paid for apprenticeship, creating an early-career pipeline problem with no clear fix.
Teaching is a caring profession unlikely to be replaced by AI, and weaker entry-level white-collar options could strengthen teacher recruitment.
quotes: Whatever you think of AI’s potential upsides—and I believe they are significant—the most urgent questions around artificial intelligence in education have to do with minimizing harm.
Jobs that amount to a single routine task, or even a bundle of routine tasks, can and will be automated.

If, therefore, you spend a lot of time sitting in meetings, working toward decisions with colleagues and clients, selling to customers, or solving problems, then good news: Your job will be hard to automate!

But to use AI effectively—especially to spot errors or misjudgments—we need people who possess deep domain expertise. That means fully developing students’ cognitive capacities and helping them become experts in something.
Concerns about early career pipelines are real, legitimate, and hard to solve.
But if AI can do many of the junior-level tasks as well or better than junior workers, this model breaks down. It’s hard for firms to charge dearly for the labor of their junior employees.

Unless you think AIs are set to become very effective at teaching most students (which I do not, in no small part due to the motivation problem), we will still need humans to help students learn, grow, and develop.
